item.title: With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?

Texas has been one of the most welcoming states for data centers, but that might change with a new governor coming in.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Under Republican Governor Greg Abbott, Texas has been one of the country's most welcoming states for new data centers. Times have changed. Abbott lost his bid for reelection, and Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has other ideas about data centers. Leigh Walden of member station KUT in Austin reports.

LEIGH WALDEN, BYLINE: Kate Goodrich is a lobbyist for the tech industry at K&L Gates, a law firm in Austin. And in the days after the election, people in her business were absorbing the change like everyone else.

KATE GOODRICH: The majority of everyone that we're talking to on both sides of the aisle have their mouths somewhere between 1 and 3 inches open still.

WALDEN: Their clients range from individual data center developers to some of the multibillion-dollar companies that operate them, like Microsoft. In November of last year, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared the state the epicenter of AI development. He has signed laws that made large data centers exempt from sales taxes for the equipment they buy. But then this summer, as he campaigned for a fourth term, he changed his tune and said it was time for Texas to start...

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GREG ABBOTT: ...Pushing back against these AI data centers that are trying to build in our neighborhoods.

WALDEN: As the public backlash to data centers grew, he also imposed a pause on all new data center projects while the state studied their impact. That pause has already expired. Meanwhile, Democrat Gina Hinojosa said this on CNN right after her surprising victory for governor.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GINA HINOJOSA: Right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.

WALDEN: Now people are watching for what she's going to do as the issue plays out across the country after the midterms. Incoming governors in Kansas and Georgia also promise to pause data centers. But because of the size of its economy, Texas often sets a precedent for how other states do business too. John Hall is the CEO and president of Houston Advanced Research Center, which focuses on environmental policy. He expects Hinojosa to impose a moratorium and then new regulations.

JOHN HALL: Establish it in policy that data centers should have to bring their own water and bring their own power. But in addition to that, offset their emissions.

WALDEN: Austin McCarty, a tech lobbyist at K&L Gates, said some of his clients are okay with more regulation. They think it might build trust and actually improve the industry's reputation.

AUSTIN MCCARTY: It's being dragged down by some folks that are not as prepared as the good actors who have really put in a lot of work to show that they're here to be a part of a really important ecosystem here in Texas.

WALDEN: Some Texans, though skeptical, seem willing to let the industry work on what they see as making amends. Torrie Martin is a horse rancher outside of San Marcos in Central Texas. She's gone to numerous local government meetings to speak against a proposed data center site near her ranch.

TORRIE MARTIN: I am optimistic, but, you know, we have to hold people accountable and pay attention to what is happening.

WALDEN: She thinks it's because of the unpopularity of data centers that laws will be passed and bipartisan agreements reached.

MARTIN: People on either side or all sides are fighting the same fight, which makes me feel more confident in my decision to, you know, stand up so loudly for the ranch lands and agricultural side to Texas.

WALDEN: New state lawmakers will be sworn in January, and then they'll begin a legislative session where data centers will be on the agenda.

From NPR News, I'm Leigh Walden in Austin.

item.title: Postmortem of AI ads
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Postmortem of AI ads

The data AI companies have been accumulating in this cycle will help serve future ads to hyper-specific audiences.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The midterm election was a big moment for AI political advertising. Campaigns spent at least $187 million on ads, either generated or enhanced by artificial intelligence. That's according to the nonpartisan Wesleyan Media Project. These ads did not appear to affect the overall outcomes of this election, but that's not going to stop campaigns from making more of them in the next cycle. NPR political reporter Maham Javaid has more.

MAHAM JAVAID, BYLINE: Many New York voters saw a spot featuring an AI-generated avatar of Governor Kathy Hochul earlier this year. It's a deepfake, where she appears in various settings, like in front of a windmill and a hotel lobby, saying...

(SOUNDBITE OF AD)

AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) We provided luxury accommodations for illegal migrants in beautiful hotels just like this.

JAVAID: The ad, which came with an AI disclaimer, was paid for by Hochul's Republican opponent for the gubernatorial seat, Bruce Blakeman.

(SOUNDBITE OF AD)

AI-GENERATED VOICE: (As Kathy Hochul) This November, don't let Bruce Blakeman lower your taxes or make New York safe. Keep it unsafe and unaffordable with Kathy Hochul as your governor.

JAVAID: Hochul won the race handily by roughly 20 points. More than 90% of the millions of dollars spent on AI ads were supporting Republican candidates, many of whom lost. The ads often did not connect with voters, says Basil Smikle, a Democratic strategist. But he says campaigns will keep using them.

BASIL SMIKLE: You could create an ad that has a lot more shock value than a typical live-action video and produce them more quickly.

JAVAID: They're also much cheaper, says GOP strategist Brian Ruddle.

BRIAN RUDDLE: If you're a candidate who does not have a big budget, can't go out and hire a television production company, but you've got a good message and something that can break through.

JAVAID: That's where AI can help, Ruddle says. And as the technology gets better, it'll get harder to detect what is real.

RUDDLE: It is not just about convincing some people that fake things are real. Sometimes it's about people thinking that real things are now fake.

JAVAID: Jason Riley is a retired Navy pilot from Austin, Texas. He says this time around, the AI ads he saw didn't fool him or sway his vote. But about 61% of Americans are concerned that audio or video deepfakes did affect the election's outcome. That's according to the UC San Diego Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. Some voters are concerned about the technology's ability to misguide them, including Steve Geller (ph), a book editor from Sacramento, California.

STEVE GELLER: I think it's not worth having a society which allows this, even though I do think it can be effective for a politician to use it.

JAVAID: This cycle, AI collected a lot of voter data, which could be useful to campaigns, says Brendan Steinhauser, another GOP strategist.

BRENDAN STEINHAUSER: AI-generated ads that are running to specific individuals based on their behavior online.

JAVAID: That means, he says, very targeted ads at scale that are going to be more effective over time.

Maham Javaid, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF TOMMY GUERRERO'S "BY THE SEA AT THE END OF THE WORLD")

item.title: Chen Jining: The Tragedy of the ‘Potential Successor’ in Chinese Politics
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Nowadays, political purges in China are nothing new. However, the announcement of an investigation into Shanghai Party Secretary Chen Jining on the night of November 24 still came as a surprise. A model technocrat in charge of China’s economic stronghold, Chen was widely regarded by China watchers as a potential successor to Xi Jinping.

While initially shocking, Chen’s downfall is not overwhelmingly surprising given the continued instability among Chinese political elites. In fact, a survey of the history of comparable regime types suggests that such potential successors are rarely immune to political pitfalls. In some sense, Chen’s case echoes previous instances under communist leaders of similar caliber, like Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong.

A review of Stalin and Mao’s relations with their potential or designated successors reveals a history of rocky relations. Stalin was infamous for initiating mass purges to weed out “counter-revolutionaries,” “plotters,” and “saboteurs,” labels used to target any perceived sign of disloyalty or ideological deviation. Throughout his rule, Stalin purged anyone who might pose a threat to his authority, regardless of their personal relations with him. Under Stalin, anyone could become an “enemy of the people” overnight; his victims include longtime followers, hatchet men, potential successors, and their associates.

Toward the end of his life, Stalin became increasingly suspicious of those around him. While he never formally designated a successor, his deputy Andrei Zhdanov was considered a likely successor until their relationship grew distant in 1948. The Politburo sent Zhdanov to a sanatorium, where he died from a cardiac arrest soon after. After Zhdanov’s passing, Stalin’s lackeys investigated his underlings in Leningrad and several were executed by shooting, with more imprisoned or sent into exile. The ruthless repression of his confidants indicates that Stalin harbored deep-seated suspicions about Zhdanov’s political network.

Following the Leningrad Affair, Stalin oversaw the Mingrelian Affair that began in 1951, which targeted Lavrentiy Beria, the powerful secret police chief and another possible successor to Stalin. Fortunately for Beria, Stalin died before the Mingrelian Affair reached to its crescendo.

Likewise, Mao treated his successors with equal, if not more, sadism. After the People’s Republic’s establishment in 1949, Mao initially used his deputy and possible successor Gao Gang to attack another potential successor, Liu Shaoqi, before abandoning Gao when his political maneuvers went overboard. Gao committed suicide in 1954 to escape from the subsequent political humiliation rituals.

Although Mao and Liu Shaoqi maintained working relations for the next few years, their relations soured following Liu’s criticism against Mao’s Great Leap Forward in 1962. In the subsequent years, Mao grew increasingly suspicious of Liu’s expanding political influence, which drove Mao to launch the Cultural Revolution with Liu as the main target. Liu died from mental and physical torture in 1969.

Lin Biao, who succeeded Liu as Mao’s designated successor, came into conflict with Mao after the active phase of the Cultural Revolution. While Lin wanted more political security, Mao believed Lin already wielded enough power. Fearing an impending purge, Lin fled China in 1971 but died when his plane crashed in Mongolia.

Although never designated as Mao’s successor, Deng Xiaoping was widely regarded a capable cadre and a frontrunner to succeed him. Nonetheless, Deng was purged twice: first during the opening of the Cultural Revolution and once more in 1976, when he tried to reverse some of its excess. Wang Hongwen, a Cultural Revolution rebel faction leader, was groomed for a year to be Mao’s successor, then sidelined due to his incompetence.

Toward the end of his life, Mao eventually settled on Hua Guofeng as his heir apparent. However, had Mao lived longer, it is very much possible that Hua, too, might have fallen victim to a purge, particularly because his status as Mao’s successor would have attracted a political following among the elite – one that would inevitably have elicited misgivings from the Helmsman.

Although no autocrat can govern alone, the accumulation of authority by capable subordinates can create suspicion and ultimately lead to confrontations. As illustrated in the above examples, potential or designated successors in these political systems enjoy little protection from the ire of the supreme leader. Competence in a successor is not exactly a virtue, but can be a source of distrust, as it poses a challenge to the incumbent leader’s standing.

We may not know the precise reasons behind Chen Jining’s purge for some time, but there is certainly more to the story than the terse official explanation of “severe violations of discipline and law.” Judging from historical precedents, Chen’s status and reputation may have triggered Xi’s suspicion, leading to his removal.

Over the years, prominent politicians, CEOs, and academics who knew Chen have publicly praised him in front of the Chinese media as a young, competent technocrat and a possible future leader of China. Yet outside observers overlooked a crucial point: only Xi can determine who succeeds him, regardless of foreign opinions and declarations. In this system characterized by highly personalized authority, Xi exercises absolute power over the rise and fall of officials. International support for Chen might have hurt rather than helped his image in Xi’s eyes.…
